Hi there, I’m so glad you’re here. I really appreciate you taking the time to meet with me today. I’m here to listen, to understand, and to support you in whatever way feels most meaningful for you right now.  

What’s been on your mind or bringing you in today?

I’ve been feeling really overwhelmed lately—like I’m back in that place where my body just starts shaking without warning, even when I’m sitting still. It started after the stomach virus, and suddenly everything feels like it’s coming back. I don’t know if it’s just the illness or if I’m really feeling the anxiety again, but it’s like the panic is waking up and it’s not going away. I keep thinking about how I used to feel like that as a kid, and now I’m 19 and it’s happening again. It’s scary, and I don’t know if I can handle it all on my own.

It sounds like you're carrying a deep sense of overwhelm—like your body is reacting to something long buried, even after just a simple illness. The shaking, the way it feels like you're back in that childhood place, that’s not just a physical reaction; it’s a signal that your nervous system is remembering something it’s been trying to protect itself from. And the fear that you can’t handle it all on your own? That’s real, and it’s completely valid. You don’t have to carry it alone. Would it be helpful to explore what that childhood memory might have been, or what part of this feeling you want to name first?

I remember when I was six, I had a panic attack in the middle of the playground—my heart was pounding so hard I thought I was going to pass out. I still have that memory, like a shadow. I used to hide in the bathroom, and I’d just keep breathing until it passed. It didn’t feel like I was in control. Now, with the stomach virus, it’s like the panic is coming back, and it’s not just the body—it’s the same fear, the same way my chest tightens and I can’t stop shaking. I used to think it was just me, but now I wonder if it’s something deeper. I’ve been trying meditation and medication, and they help, but when the virus hits, it feels like everything just cracks open again. I don’t know if I’m ready to face it, but I’m not sure I can keep pushing through it alone either.

It sounds like that six-year-old moment in the playground—something so vivid and terrifying—has been living under the surface, and now, with the virus, it’s finally surfaced again. The fact that your body remembers that panic, even after all these years, shows how deeply that experience was felt and how much it shaped your nervous system. It’s not just a memory; it’s a pattern that keeps showing up when your body feels unsafe. And you’re right to feel scared—this isn’t just a temporary reaction. It’s a signal that you’re still carrying that fear, and it’s okay to feel it. Would it be helpful to explore what part of that moment you’re still feeling now, or what part of today’s feeling feels most like the old one?

I think about that moment in the playground and it still makes my chest tighten, like I’m back there—cold, alone, and completely out of control. I don’t know if I’m ready to face it, but I do know that when I feel that tightness now, it’s not just my body—it’s like a piece of me is still trying to protect itself from what happened back then. I keep wondering if I’ll ever feel safe enough to truly let go of that fear. But maybe, just maybe, if I can name it, breathe through it, and stay with it without running, I can start to feel like I’m in my own body again. I don’t know if that’s possible, but I’d like to try.

I still feel that coldness in my chest when I think about the playground—like something is waiting to catch me off guard. Even now, with the virus, it’s not just the shaking or the panic; it feels like the fear is coming back to life, and I can’t tell if it’s just my body or if it’s actually remembering what happened. I used to think medication and breathing helped me get through it, but now I wonder if they’re just covering the surface. I don’t want to run from it, but I’m scared that if I face it, I’ll feel broken again. I’d really like to try staying with it—just for a little while—without trying to fix it or push it away. Maybe that’s where healing starts.
